title: Eid al-Adha: days of tashriq
hookLine: takbir after prayers for the days after Eid

lines: DID THE THIRD FLOOR GET THEIRS?
A FEAST THAT DOESN'T END IN A DAY.
cards: In a lot of Muslim homes, the morning of Eid al-Adha has a particular sound.
Not just greetings and children, but bags: plastic bags of meat divided on the kitchen counter, knotted, labeled, carried next door, driven across town, handed to the man who sweeps the street.
Phones buzzing with addresses. Someone always asking whether the neighbors on the third floor got theirs. It's the feast of the sacrifice, and it doesn't end in one day.

teach.b: Eid al-Adha falls on the tenth of Dhul Hijjah, the day after the pilgrims stand at 'Arafah.
It remembers Ibrahim, who in Surah As-Saffat saw in a dream that he was to sacrifice his son, and both of them submitted, and God ransomed the son with a tremendous sacrifice.

teach.h: EAT, AND FEED THE ONE WHO ASKS.
teach.b: Muslims who are able offer an animal, a sheep, a goat, a share in a cow or camel, and the Qur'an tells them in Surah Al-Hajj to eat of it and to feed the one who is content and the one who asks.
Many divide it in thirds: for the household, for friends and neighbors, and for those in need, a custom scholars recommend rather than require.
The same surah adds a line often quoted at Eid: neither the flesh nor the blood reaches God; what reaches Him is your devotion, your taqwa.
Then come three more days, the eleventh, twelfth and thirteenth, called the days of tashriq.

A hadith in Sahih Muslim describes them in a phrase that became today's line: they are days of eating and drinking, and of remembering God. Fasting is not allowed on them. And the remembrance has a shape.
Surah Al-Baqarah says to remember God through the numbered days, and many Muslims say the takbir after each of the five daily prayers, from the dawn of 'Arafah until the afternoon of the thirteenth.
It begins: God is greatest, God is greatest, there is no god but God. The schools differ a little on the exact start and end.
A feast, a share for the neighbor, and a refrain after every prayer, across the four days of the feast.

how: On Eid al-Adha Muslims who are able offer an animal sacrifice and share the meat with family, neighbors and people in need; many say the takbir after the daily prayers through the days of tashriq, the eleventh to thirteenth of Dhul Hijjah.

o: the feast that marks the end of Ramadan's fast
the pilgrims' day of standing on the plain
the feast of the sacrifice, remembering Ibrahim

s: the days of tashriq are good days for a voluntary fast
the hadith calls them days of eating, drinking and remembering God; fasting isn't allowed.
the Qur'an says the sacrifice's flesh and blood don't reach God
Surah Al-Hajj says what reaches Him is the devotion.
dividing the meat in thirds is a strict obligation
it's a common custom that scholars recommend, not a requirement.

games.q: it's Eid morning. the meat is divided. one bag is left, and you haven't decided. who gets it?
o: the one who asks, or a neighbor in need.
nobody; give money instead next year.
games.why: Surah Al-Hajj says eat of it and feed the content and the one who asks; many keep a third aside for people in need.

practice: Picture the people who live closest to you: the door across the hall, the house over the fence, the colleague at the next desk.
Pick one, maybe someone you've never really spoken to, and think what you could bring them; it needn't be meat or anything grand, just a plate of something you cooked or a box of fruit.
If you pray, you can say God is greatest, quietly, as you picture handing it over.

wordCard.voice: Eid al-Adha. The feast of the sacrifice on the tenth of Dhul Hijjah, remembering Ibrahim's ransom, followed by the three days of tashriq. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the days of tashriq, the three days after Eid al-Adha, the eleventh to the thirteenth of Dhul Hijjah.

carryVoice: Your line: eat, drink, remember. A feast that keeps a refrain going. Day five hundred fourteen, done.

sources.ref: Qur'an 22:36–37 (eat and feed; the devotion reaches Him)
Qur'an 2:203 (remember God through the numbered days)
Sahih Muslim 1141 (days of eating, drinking and remembrance)
